newsitem.title: GERMANY: German coalition agrees tax cut in principle.
newsitem.headline: German coalition agrees tax cut in principle.

text.p: Germany's three-party coalition government has agreed in principle to make a two-point cut in the solidarity surcharge, a tax raised to aid east German reconstruction, from 1998, sources said on Thursday.

Demands by junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) for the cut in the 7.5 percent levy threatened to wreck Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government, but the sources said a final decision on the cut would only be taken in mid-December.

The deal, reached on Tuesday, has cleared the air in the fractious governing alliance, which is now seeking to close a gap of three billion marks in its 1997 budget, and qualify for European monetary union.
Final talks on a cut in the solidarity tax next month would also be tied in with coalition negotiations on a major overhaul of Germany's labyrinthine tax system.

The FDP has pressed for the tax reform to take effect in 1998 -- an election year -- but Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and Finance Minister Theo Waigel's Christian Social Union (CSU) want to introduce the reform in 1999.

A coalition row had broken out after mounting financial woes forced the coalition to put off a planned one-point cut in the solidarity tax next year -- leading to FDP calls for a bigger cut to compensate in 1998.
